title: Sin embargo and no obstante: contrast between ideas

sections.content: You know contrast connectors such as *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1. They begin a new sentence (after a full stop or a semicolon) and are followed by a comma. They tell the reader that the second idea goes against what the first made you expect. The Cold War in Central America is full of such contrasts: what the United States did, and what was said against it.

items.spanish: Estados Unidos dio ayuda militar al gobierno de El Salvador. Sin embargo, esa ayuda fue muy criticada.
items.english: The United States gave military aid to the government of El Salvador. However, that aid was heavily criticised.

items.spanish: El Congreso limitó la ayuda a los contras. No obstante, algunos funcionarios siguieron buscando dinero para ellos.
items.english: Congress limited the aid to the Contras. Nevertheless, some officials kept looking for money for them.

items.spanish: La intervención de Estados Unidos fue importante. Sin embargo, las causas de las guerras eran también internas.
items.english: The intervention of the United States was important. However, the causes of the wars were also internal.

items.spanish: Reagan hablaba de comunismo. Los críticos, sin embargo, hablaban de pobreza.
items.english: Reagan spoke about communism. The critics, however, spoke about poverty.

sections.content: *Sin embargo* can also sit in the middle of a sentence, between commas (*los críticos, sin embargo, hablaban…*). Do not add *pero* next to it: *sin embargo* already does the job. *No obstante* is a little more formal.
